svg.title: EIGRP: the three tables, the three terms that decide local repair, and a worked feasible-successor example
svg.desc: Three table cards on the left: the neighbour table holds adjacencies and is the transport table; the topology table holds every route every neighbour has offered, with reported distance and feasible distance per entry; the routing table holds only the successors that were selected. Three terms are defined in the middle: reported distance, the neighbour's own cost to the destination; feasible distance, this router's total cost through that neighbour, equal to reported distance plus the link cost; and feasible successor, a neighbour whose reported distance is strictly less than the current feasible distance, because that inequality proves the neighbour is not routing back through us. The worked example: the current best path has feasible distance 1000 via neighbour A, neighbour B reports 800, so 800 is less than 1000, B is a feasible successor and the repair is immediate and local, with no query sent. A note explains that without a feasible successor, DUAL must query, and once a query starts it can spread across the whole autonomous system.
svg.text: EIGRP is three tables and one inequality; the inequality is what makes it fast
A feasible successor means recovery with no protocol conversation at all — the rest of the design is about keeping that true

A prefix here but not there is a DUAL decision, not a bug.

FD = 1000 · this path is up and installed
B is a feasible successor. Link A fails → B installs
immediately. No query, no wait, no network-wide event.
Why the inequality works: if B's cost to the destination were greater than or equal to yours, B could be reaching it through you —
which would make B a loop, not an alternative. Requiring RD < FD is a loop-freedom proof, computed locally, with no topology knowledge.
